summary: This document defines new DLEP Data Items and messages for credit-based flow control. Credit windows regulate when data may be sent into an associated virtual or physical queue.

plainLanguage.summary: You may only send as many items as you have tickets. The receiver hands out tickets so its queue never overflows.

questions: what is dlep credit window flow control
what are dlep message types 17 and 18
how does a dlep router request more credits
what is a flow identifier in dlep
subtitle: How a DLEP modem hands out byte credits so a router never overruns the modem's queues.

tldr.problem: DLEP does not include any flow control, so a router can send traffic to a modem that has no buffer space for it.
tldr.mechanism: The modem advertises one credit window per flow, measured in octets, and grants more credit as it frees queue space. The router spends credits for each packet it sends and must not send when none remain. Two new messages and five new Data Items carry the credits.
tldr.outcome: Credit-based flow control is proactive, so packet loss from insufficient buffer space is less likely than with a pause mechanism. The messages and Data Items are reusable by extensions such as RFC 9894.

today: RFC 9893 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It supplies the common credit messages and Data Items that extensions such as RFC 9894 build on.

sections.title: Why DLEP Needs Credits
sections.content:
The Dynamic Link Exchange Protocol (DLEP, RFC 8175) lets a router and a modem exchange link information. It does not identify flows beyond DLEP endpoints and has no flow control. A pause mechanism exists in RFC 8651, but this document defines a credit scheme instead.

Credit-based flow control is proactive: the transmitter does not send packets until the receiver says there is enough buffer space. That makes packet loss from insufficient buffer space less likely than with a pause mechanism. Using other flow control mechanisms at the same time is out of scope.

Flow control here covers only traffic sent from the router to the modem. The RFC defines two new messages and five new Data Items. They are common and reusable, and other DLEP extensions are expected to need them, such as the one in RFC 9894.
sections.plainLanguage: A router wants to send lots of data to a modem, but the modem only has so much room. The modem gives out permission slips so the router never sends more than fits.

sections.title: Credit Windows, Flows and Classifiers
sections.content:
Credits are managed per logical credit window, and each window can be thought of as a queue inside the modem. There is a direct one-to-one mapping between credit windows and flows, identified by Flow Identifiers (FIDs) carried in the Traffic Classification Data Item of RFC 9892. Traffic Classification Identifiers (TIDs) group those flows. TID and FID values mean something only to the modem that issued them.

When a destination becomes reachable, the modem associates a TID with it. The router finds the FID within that TID that matches a packet, and so finds the credit window. Windows can therefore be shared across destinations or dedicated to one, whichever suits the modem's implementation.

Along with the classification, the modem gives an initial credit window size and the maximum size of the associated queue. The maximum is included for informative and potential future uses. Credits flow only one way: they are never provided by the router to the modem.

Modems must map the overhead of their own transmission technology onto the credit semantics, because credits include per-frame MAC headers. The modem may need to approximate.

When credit windowing is used, a router MUST NOT send data traffic to a modem if no classifier matches the packet. If a classifier matches, the router MUST NOT send when the associated credit window has no credits. It must make sure there are enough credits for the whole packet first.

Credits are counted in octets, and the count includes MAC overhead. For Ethernet, framing, header and trailer are all included. The window is decremented by the number of octets sent.

If a packet matches nothing and the modem did not provide a wildcard, the packet MUST be dropped by the router.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each kind of traffic gets its own jar of tickets. A label on each package tells the router which jar to take a ticket from.

Before the router sends a package, it checks that it has enough tickets for the whole package, including the wrapping paper.

sections.title: The Two Credit Messages
sections.content:
Both new messages must be sent and received to support credit windows. Credit Control has Message Type 17 and Credit Control Response is 18.

Both modems and routers can send a Credit Control Message, but a sender MUST NOT send another until it has received a Credit Control Response from its peer. A modem's message MUST contain one or more Credit Window Grant Data Items to increase windows, and the router MUST respond. A router's message MUST contain one or more Credit Window Request Data Items and SHOULD contain a Credit Window Status Data Item for each request.

A router sends a Credit Control Response with one or more Credit Window Status Data Items. A modem's response MUST contain a Grant Data Item for every request in the message it answers, and each grant MAY add zero or more credits.
sections.plainLanguage: One side says "here are more tickets" or "I need more tickets". The other side must answer before the first can say anything new.

sections.title: The Five Data Items
sections.content:
Each Data Item has a type, a length and these fields. A wrong length makes the item corrupt, so the message cannot be reliably parsed and is ignored. Other parsing errors terminate the session with a Status Data Item of "Invalid Data".

  • Credit Window Initialization (30, length 16): sent by the modem to identify a window by FID, give a 64-bit Credit Value in octets, a Scale (0 bytes, 1 KB, 2 MB, 3 GB) and a 24-bit Credit Window Max Size. It SHOULD appear in any Session Initialization Response that indicates support, and updates MAY go in Session Update Messages.
  • Credit Window Association (31, length 2): carries a TID, in every Destination Up and Destination Update Message from the modem. A TID is not used unless listed here.
  • Credit Window Grant (32, length 12): the modem adds Additional Credits, a 64-bit octet count, to the window for a FID. Zero means none are added.
  • Credit Window Status (33, length 12): the router reports the Current Credit Window Size, a 64-bit octet count.
  • Credit Window Request (34, variable length): the router lists FIDs, 2 octets each, whose windows need credits. The value 0xFFFF means all FIDs.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five kinds of notes: set up a jar, say which jars a destination uses, give tickets, tell how many tickets are left, and ask for more tickets.

sections.title: How Routers and Modems Process Credits
sections.content:
On a Credit Window Initialization, the router checks that the FID was provided in a Traffic Classification Data Item. If not, it SHOULD log this. It then creates the window, or updates an existing one. If the credit value would exceed the Credit Window Max Size, the maximum becomes the window size. Windows can shrink, for example after a transmission rate change. Then the modem SHOULD NOT issue more credit for that FID until the window has drained below the new maximum.

On a Grant, the router increases the window by the Additional Credits, capped at the maximum. Windows are managed independently of the destination named in the carrying message. For a Grant in any message other than a Credit Control Response, the router MUST report the result in a Credit Window Status Data Item. This goes in the Destination Up Response for a Destination Up, otherwise in a Credit Control Message.

On a Status, the modem SHOULD compare the reported size with what it expects. If the difference is more than observed data frames explain, it SHOULD send an Initialization Data Item to reset the window. For small differences, it MAY adjust later grants. On a Request, the modem MUST answer with Grant Data Items in a new Credit Control Message. Unknown FIDs SHOULD be logged and ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router's count of tickets drifts away from the modem's count, the modem tells the router the right number so they agree again.

sections.title: Management and Compatibility
sections.content:
Modems MAY allow the number of advertised credit windows to be configured. Routers may have limits on queues, and per-destination queues may not be supported at all. If a modem offers more than the router can handle, the router SHOULD use a subset, or MAY reset the session and say the extension is not supported. Either way the mismatch SHOULD be reported through normal management mechanisms. In all cases, traffic without credits MUST NOT be sent to the modem.

The messages and Data Items are only used when an extension requires them. Unexpected appearances of any Data Item are handled as RFC 8175 specifies.
sections.plainLanguage: If the router cannot keep track of as many jars as the modem offers, it uses fewer, and tells a person about it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Credit window flow control exposes vulnerabilities similar to existing DLEP messages. For example, a malicious actor posing as a DLEP peer could inject a Credit Window Initialization Data Item that resizes a window so as to cause denial of service.

The transport-layer security mechanisms of RFC 8175, along with the latest BCP 195, can be applied. The Layer 2 security mechanisms in RFC 8175 can also be applied with some updates. The RFC names IEEE 802.1AE and IEEE 8802-1X as examples of technologies that can secure the link.
sections.plainLanguage: A trickster pretending to be the modem could shrink the router's jar to nothing, so the router can never send. Locks on the connection keep tricksters out.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned two Message Type values and five Data Item Type values from the Specification Required range.

RegistryCodeName
Message Type17Credit Control
Message Type18Credit Control Response
Data Item30Credit Window Initialization
Data Item31Credit Window Association
Data Item32Credit Window Grant
Data Item33Credit Window Status
Data Item34Credit Window Request
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of codes got seven new entries, one for each new message and note type.

messages.label: Traffic Classification, Association, Initialization
messages.note: Sets up flows and credit windows.

messages.label: Credit Window Grant
messages.note: More credits as packets are transmitted.

messages.label: Credit Window Status
messages.note: Router reports its view of the window.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Number of octets in the Data Item; MUST be 16.

fields.name: Flow Identifier (FID)
fields.desc: Identifies the flow and its credit window.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: MUST be all zeros; ignored on reception.

fields.name: Credit Value
fields.desc: Credits in octets to add, including MAC headers.

fields.name: Credit Window Max Size
fields.desc: Maximum window size in the unit given by Scale.
